Freak Flag
FREEK flag
noun (Boomer slang)
From Jimi Hendrix’s "If 6 Was 9" (1967): "I’m gonna wave my freak flag high," and above all from Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young’s "Almost Cut My Hair" (1970): "I feel like letting my freak flag fly." The freak flag was the long hair, beard, and wild dress that marked a man as one of the counterculture’s "freaks" — a word the hippies had reclaimed as a badge. Let your freak flag fly is still used for openly displaying one’s eccentricity.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

One’s freak flag is the visible sign of being different — in 1970, the long hair that said "I am not one of you"; today, any eccentricity a person refuses to hide. Let your freak flag fly means: be unapologetically yourself. The Christian observation: Scripture actually calls believers to be visibly different, but it locates the difference somewhere else entirely. "Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light" (1Pe 2:9). Peculiar there means a people for God’s own possession, and their difference is meant to show forth His praises, not their own uniqueness. Paul says plainly, "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10) — there is a holy oddness, and the world will notice it. But the freak flag flies for the self. Its message is "look at me," and Proverbs has a sharp word for that impulse: "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself" (Pro 18:2). The test is the one Paul applies to himself: "do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The hippie refused to please his parents and sought instead to please his peers. The Christian refuses to make pleasing men his aim at all. That is a flag worth flying.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer slang (Hendrix 1967; CSNY 1970) for the long hair or wild dress that marked a counterculture "freak"; hence any proudly displayed eccentricity — a self-display Scripture sets against the "peculiar people" who show forth God’s praises (1Pe 2:9).

FREAK FLAG, n. (Boomer slang, 1967–70) The long hair, beard, or flamboyant dress by which a hippie ("freak") displayed his rejection of mainstream society; hence any outward sign of nonconformity. Let one’s freak flag fly — to display one’s eccentricity openly and without apology.

Webster (1828) — FLAG, noun An ensign or colors; a cloth on which are usually painted or wrought certain figures, and borne on a staff. In the army, a banner by which one regiment is distinguished from another. In the marine, a banner or standard by which the ships of one nation are distinguished from those of another, or by which an admiral is distinguished from other ships of his squadron. In the British navy, an admiral’s flag is displayed at the main-top-gallant-mast-head, a vice-admiral’s at the fore-top-gallant-mast-head, and a rear-admiral’s at the mizen-top-gallant-mast-head. To strike or lower the flag, is to pull it down upon the cap in token of respect or submission. To strike the flag in an engagement, is the sign of surrendering. To hang out the white flag, is to ask quarter; or in some cases, to manifest a friendly design. The red flag, is a sign of defiance or battle.

Decode for families: the modern equivalent is "authenticity" — the self as the thing displayed.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:9 — "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:"

1Co 4:10 — "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised."

Pro 18:2 — "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself."

Gal 1:10 — "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ."

Rom 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

Modern Corruption

The freak flag makes nonconformity a display of the self; Scripture calls believers to a holy peculiarity that displays the praises of God and refuses to make pleasing men — old or young — the aim.

expand to see more

The freak flag was sold as courage — the brave individual against the gray conformist crowd. But the long-haired young man of 1970 was usually conforming exactly, to a different crowd. The flag was a uniform. That is the irony of every self-expression movement: it ends in a new set of rules about how to look different. Paul saw through it: the question is never whether you please men but which men, unless you have decided to please God (Gal 1:10).

Christian nonconformity is real and commanded: "be not conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2). But it is not achieved by hair, dress, or attitude; it is produced by a renewed mind. Its visible marks are the strangest things the world ever sees — a man who forgives, a woman who is content, a family that keeps the Lord’s Day, a young person who will not lie. Those are the peculiar people of 1Pe 2:9, and their flag is the cross.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English freak (an oddity; reclaimed by 1960s hippies) + flag → Hendrix "If 6 Was 9" (1967), CSNY "Almost Cut My Hair" (1970) → let your freak flag fly.

expand to see more

English freak — an oddity of nature; in 1960s slang, a hippie or an enthusiast ("jazz freak")

English flag — a banner, a standard, an ensign of allegiance

1967: Jimi Hendrix, "If 6 Was 9" — "wave my freak flag high"

1970: Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, "Almost Cut My Hair" — "let my freak flag fly"

Scripture: the "peculiar people" (1Pe 2:9) — God’s own possession, displaying His praises

Usage

""Grandpa let his freak flag fly until he got a job at the bank in ’72.""

"Ye are a peculiar people, to shew forth His praises (1Pe 2:9) — not your own."

"If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ (Gal 1:10)."
